request.query: Continue the same account search, finding up to THREE ADDITIONAL distinct companies beyond Trainline and Ocado. Try technical customer case studies, engineering talks and company engineering blogs for travel, online retail, gaming or SaaS companies operating distributed production Kubernetes with their own engineers. Preserve ALL required company conditions from the prior request. Prefer reachable firms over global giants. Confirm company headcount and headquarters at the company identity level. Fewer is valid, but first try a different retrieval angle when a promising candidate lacks evidence.
request.systemPrompt:
Today is 2026-09-06. The account's exact instructions are authoritative: This profile is for Trust Fabric only, not Form3's payments platform. Form3 (form3.tech) sells Trust Fabric, a product installed into a Kubernetes cluster to manage certificate trust and infrastructure risk across distributed services.
Hard gates, all required: runs production Kubernetes with a distributed architecture or many independent services (no cluster, no deal); an in-house engineering team operates that infrastructure, not an outsourced platform; 501 or more employees; uptime-critical or regulated, where an hour of downtime is a board-level event; based in North America, the UK and Ireland, or Continental Europe. Do not gate on revenue.
Verticals: SaaS, online retail, fintech, automotive, energy, pharma, gaming, media, travel, telcos, public sector. Model accounts at reachable size: Trainline, Skyscanner, Auto Trader UK, Ocado Technology, Deliveroo.
Out: consultants, agencies, non-profits, private equity, recruiters, freelancers, managed service providers and systems integrators, and certificate-lifecycle vendors such as AppViewX, Entrust and CyberArk.
The buyer is the platform, infrastructure or security leader who owns the cluster and its certificate estate, never the payments or commercial function: CTO, CIO, CISO, and the VP, Director or Head of Engineering, Platform Engineering, Infrastructure, Cloud, Site Reliability Engineering, DevOps, Security Engineering, Information Security or Architecture. CEO only at companies under about 1,000 people. Exclude recruiters, HR, sales, marketing, individual engineers and academics. At most three people per company.
Hot signals: a platform, SRE, infrastructure or PKI role posted in the last 30 days naming Kubernetes, TLS, mTLS, cert-manager, PKI or a service mesh; public evidence of production Kubernetes at scale; a published SLA; DORA, PSD2, NIS2 or PCI DSS obligations; a new platform or security leader in the last 12 months; a post-quantum commitment; a public certificate or TLS incident in the last 90 days.

This task finds companies only. Buyer titles guide later people selection, not a new company gate. Preserve company-versus-parent identity. Cite source URLs and short verbatim quotes for every required condition and for the company LinkedIn URL. Distinguish an event date from publication date. Unknown evidence stays unknown. Never infer employee count from customer count. Do not invent URLs or dates. A skills list on a personal profile does not establish that a job was posted recently or that its employer currently operates that technology. A profile's crawl/update date is not a job-post publication date. Cite the actual job detail or event page for optional dated signals; otherwise leave those unproven. Copy a contiguous verbatim quote without inserting ellipses; use several evidence entries when separate passages are needed.

output.text: Three additional companies are delivered: Skyscanner, Auto Trader UK and John Lewis Partnership. All have evidence for production Kubernetes, distributed or multi-service architectures, in-house engineering ownership, at least 501 employees, qualifying headquarters and uptime-sensitive travel, automotive-marketplace or online-retail operations. Optional SLA, named regulatory, post-quantum and recent certificate/TLS-incident signals remain unproven where no sufficiently direct evidence was found.

companies.description: Skyscanner is an Edinburgh-based travel-search platform operating a large, distributed Kubernetes estate for its own travel-search services.
companies.selectionReason: Strongest additional reachable travel fit: the evidence explicitly establishes 24 production Kubernetes clusters, more than 1,000 microservices, platform-engineer ownership, 1,313 employees and Edinburgh headquarters. Its very large user and travel-provider footprint makes uptime operationally consequential, although no public SLA or named regulatory obligation was established.

The company also publicly describes a platform responsible for 24/7 availability; the case study's 55 million monthly visits support the uptime-critical gate.

companies.description: John Lewis Partnership is a London-headquartered UK retailer whose Digital Platform runs customer-facing e-commerce workloads on Google Kubernetes Engine through an internal platform-engineering organization.
companies.selectionReason: Qualifies as a large UK online-retail account with a documented internal Digital Platform, GKE foundation, customer-facing production services and 3,177 employees at London headquarters. The £2.5bn annual online platform makes availability commercially material. It is less reachable than Auto Trader and Skyscanner because of its larger partnership and supplier ecosystem, but remains a strong technical fit.
